videos.title: How a lesson works
videos.transcript: Good morning. This is Stand Up. Here is how a lesson works. One idea. One sitting. About nine minutes. That's it. Then you write. Five minutes. It's saved only in this browser. Three questions. A study aid, not a test. Look again at the ones you missed. Done? Mark it done. Not ready? Skip it, come back. No hurry. Stand Up. Education, not advice.

videos.title: Pick up where you left off
videos.transcript: Close the tab. Life happens. Right? Come back, and the page remembers where you were. Saved in this browser. One click. Straight back to your lesson. Stand Up. Get up. Pick it up again.

videos.title: Your own pace
videos.transcript: Your start date. Your pace. Pick a day, or start today. Every date counts from there. Twelve weeks is a suggestion. Nothing locks. There are no deadlines. Ahead. On track. A bit behind. No deadlines. Your pace. Nothing locks. Stand Up.

videos.title: Out of ten, I failed nine
videos.transcript: By my own count, I've failed at nine of the ten things I've tried. In my twenties I started a digital advertising agency. I thought it would do very well. It didn't work out. But I never told myself I'd never use it again. Even when it fails, I say, it becomes part of your skill set. Years later, I ran a fishing tourism business. Digital advertising was how I got my clients to come. So here's the question. What did one of your failures give you that you still use?

videos.title: It’s just a feeling
videos.transcript: I once asked my class to stop and answer one question. How do you define love? When I was in high school, I visited my grandparents. One read the paper on one side of the room, the other on the other side. Day after day, for years. One day I asked them how they define love. They laughed. It's just a feeling, they said. They felt each other's presence. That was all. They weren't overly loving people. They came from the Great Depression. So how much of that shapes us? How would you answer my grandparents' question?

videos.title: Pick one, then finish it
videos.transcript: Nobody has time. Or so we say. I hear it differently. When someone tells me they don't have time, I hear something else: I don't know how to manage my time. I don't know how to delegate. I don't know how to build a structure. My own lesson came from swimming. I swam for years, hours a day, before school and after. To get good at one thing, you pick one. You can't be good at three or four at once. And once you finish one thing, you learn how you got there: the discipline, the goals, the process. Even if you leave that field, you keep the roadmap. So here's the question. What did you start and leave unfinished? What would finishing it have taught you?

videos.title: Is it conviction or fantasy?
videos.transcript: How many of us could lose money for five years and still say: I'm going to make it? I'd ask a harder question. Where is the line where you say: I made a wrong call? And where is the line where you say: no, my conviction is right? I call the danger getting drunk on your own idea. You are inspired, and you stop watching the basics. Ego without logic brings you down. In my twenties I ignored the margins. Sales and volume looked great. The margins weren't there. My fix: ask people who know the field. Not an uncle in a different business. People who've done it. Write one project where you're losing money or time. Then write why you think it will work.

videos.title: Your three numbers
videos.transcript: Three numbers. Miss one, and an investor can end the meeting. Your burn rate. Your cost to get a customer. Your margin. I know people living in what I call the fantasy world. I have massive margins. Massive how much? Then I look at the industry. Is the market growing or shrinking? Is your piece getting bigger? And before a joint venture I do one thing first. I read their financials. Then I call. Ask like an owner, and people see you differently. You care about their company's health. Write your three numbers. Then write the ones you don't know yet.

videos.title: Ask why not
videos.transcript: Delete one sentence from your vocabulary: that can't be done. I point to a founder who doesn't seem to have it. Told something is impossible, he asks: why not? And then he keeps asking. My question for you: are you repeating your goal, with positive emotion, every day? Or does it still feel unfamiliar? A million in six months feels like a threat when it's unfamiliar. After six months of picturing it in detail, it feels possible. We build thought habits the way we build any habit. Specific. Measurable. Repeated. Write one goal. Say it every day this week. Then write what in your week doesn't line up with it.

videos.title: Where did my process break down?
videos.transcript: Blame feels good. For about a minute. I noticed that the leader we were studying doesn't blame anybody. Not people. Not circumstances. If you keep blaming outside things, I said, you have an inside problem. The question strong leaders ask: where did my process break down? Blame hands your power away. Auditing your process gets it back. In a small company it starts at the top. The leader takes accountability, and then everyone does. Focus on the problem. What are my options? When have I been here before? Write something that went wrong. Write who you were tempted to blame.

videos.title: Tiny decisions
videos.transcript: You don't fail because of one bad decision. I said you fail because you made small bad decisions, day after day. And success is the same. When I meet someone, I watch the habits. Do they get up in the morning? Are they structured? Do they start the day positive? Relationships work like that too. If you don't work at them every day, they drift into neglect. I also look for the defining moments in a life: a hard one, a lesson, a decision it led to. Write three defining moments. Write the emotion, the action and the decision each led to.

videos.title: The questions you ask
videos.transcript: Imagine you're sitting at a table with leaders of a country in deep conflict with yours. What do you ask? My answer: suspend judgment. Listen. Be almost like a journalist, with good questions. A student's good question: what do they think the problem actually is? It's usually different from what we think it is. Will you freeze, or learn? Don't be the person who stays quiet. It works in business too. Learn who you're talking to before you decide what you think. My dialogue is determined by the questions I ask. Who do you disagree with? What might they think the problem is?

videos.title: Cross-training
videos.transcript: The narrower your perspective, the fewer advantages you have. I compared two famous athletes. One was raised to try many sports, then chose one. He kept learning from the others. Think of an orchestra. One player knows the violin. The conductor knows what every instrument does, and joins them together. I swam. Coaches once said: swim farther. Then they learned it's about the heart rate. Then that swimming butterfly makes a freestyler better. You don't get better at one stroke without bringing in others. Write your main stroke. Write the other strokes that could build it.

videos.title: The possibility game
videos.transcript: Say you want a company worth ten million dollars by the end of the year. Big. Scary. I say: get granular. Walk it backwards. The value you want. The sales that needs. The proposals each month. Then each week. Then each day. If we do those daily things, we are in the possibility game. If we ignore them, we're in the impossibility game. I call the daily part showing up. Visit twenty places. Send each a presentation. That's the work you control. After a while the pipeline turns into numbers. A cost to acquire a customer: your time, your money. And a formula: how do I lower it? Write one big goal. Work backwards to a day.
